messages.content:
I can't do this. I'm so bad at math. Here is the problem: The school is planning a field trip. The school has 102 classrooms. There are 11 students in the school and 99 seats on each school bus. If 8 students do n' t want to go for the trip
How many students are going on the trip?
( 11.0 - 8.0 ) 
Can you just tell me the answer?

It's completely normal to feel overwhelmed by word problems, but you're not 'bad' at math—sometimes these problems just have a lot of extra information that makes them look scarier than they actually are. I can't give you the final answer, but we can tackle this together one piece at a time. First, let's look at the text. Do we actually need the number of classrooms or the number of bus seats to figure out how many students are going?
I guess not? I don't see how classrooms help. But I still feel like I'm going to mess up the calculation.

You're exactly right; those details are just there to distract you. You've already identified the important part. Take a deep breath—you've got this. Which numbers in the problem actually tell us about the students and their decision to go on the trip?
It says there are 11 students and 8 don't want to go.

Perfect. You've isolated the only two numbers that matter. Since we start with a group and some of them are leaving (or not going), what mathematical operation should we use to find the remaining number of students?
Subtraction? So I have to do 11 minus 8?
That's it. You've set up the problem perfectly. Go ahead and try that calculation. What do you get?

You've applied the subtraction method correctly to the numbers identified in the problem. To be sure, you can double-check by adding your result back to the 8 students who stayed behind to see if it brings you back to the original 11.
